questions.question: A patient underwent unilateral orchiectomy for a swelling in the right testis. The specimen is sent for histopathological examination, and its microscopic appearance is depicted in the image below. Which of the following statements is true regarding the diagnosis?

options.A: 3 different sizes of tumour cells are seen
options.C: Tumor cells are arranged in sheets
options.D: Tumor cells have a watery-clear cytoplasm

explanation.text: The given histopathological image shows features suggestive of testicular seminoma. Histology of seminoma: The classic seminoma cell is large and round to polyhedral with a distinct cell membrane and a large, central nucleus with one or two prominent nucleoli. The cytoplasm is clear or watery appearing and contains glycogen. The sheets are divided into poorly demarcated lobules by the septa of the fibrous tissue.

The septa show lymphocytic infiltration (T lymphocytes). Seminoma: It is the most common germ cell tumour of the testis. A similar presentation in the ovary is called dysgerminoma, and germinoma is present in the pineal gland. Incidence: Peak incidence in the fourth decade.

Genetics: Seminomas contain isochromosome 12p and express OCT3/4 & NANOG. Gross: Seminoma has a homogeneous, grey-white, lobulated cut surface, usually devoid of hemorrhage or necrosis. 3 different sizes of tumour cells (small, medium and giant cells) are seen in a case of spermatocytic seminoma. (Option A) Endodermal sinuses-like structures called Schiller-Duval bodies are present in the case of a yolk sac tumour. (Option B) Tumour cells are arranged in sheets with cleft-like spaces in case of an embryonal carcinoma. (Option C)

questions.question: Which of the following is not a germ cell tumour?

explanation.text: The classification of testicular tumours is given in the table below. Germ cell tumours Sex cord-stromal tumours Mixed Seminomatous: Seminoma. Spermatocytic seminoma. Sertoli cell tumour. Leydig cell tumour. Pure tumours. Gonadoblastoma. Non-seminomatous: Embryonal carcinoma. Choriocarcinoma. Yolk sac tumour. Teratoma.

questions.question: A 1-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic by his parents, who are concerned about the absence of his left testicle in the scrotum. On physical examination, the right testicle is palpable in the scrotum, but the left is not. All are true regarding this condition except?

options.A: It can occur in association with hypospadias.
options.B: The most common site of arrest of descent is the inguinal canal.
options.C: It is very commonly associated with a well-defined hormonal disorder.

explanation.text: Cryptorchidism: It is a complete or partial failure of the intra-abdominal testes to descend into the scrotal sac, associated with testicular dysfunction and an increased risk of testicular cancer.

It usually occurs as an isolated anomaly but may be accompanied by other genitourinary tract malformations, such as hypospadias. (Option A) The normal descent of the testes occurs in two phases: Transabdominal phase: Mediated by Mullerian inhibiting substance. Inguinoscrotal phase: Mediated by the androgen-induced release of calcitonin-related gene peptide. Sites of arrest of descent: Inguinal canal (most common). (Option B) Abdomen (uncommon).

Morphology: Gross: The testis is small, brown, and atrophic. Microscopic: Atrophic tubules with thickened basement membrane. The subsequent loss of spermatogonia leaves the tubules with only Sertoli cells. The Leydig cells are spared and appear relatively prominent. (Option D) Management: During the first year of life, most inguinal cryptorchid testes descend spontaneously into the scrotum.
If it remains undescended, surgical correction by orchiopexy (placement in the scrotal sac) is required, preferably before the development of histologic changes (to be performed at 6-12 months).

questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of the vaginal epithelium?

explanation.text: Layers of vaginal epithelium: Cells Functions Superficial layer It forms the outermost protective barrier, eventually shed from the surface. Intermediate layer Provide structural support to the epithelium and contribute to the thickness and resilience of the vaginal tissue. Parabasal layer Serve as transitional cells between the basal and intermediate layers, reflecting ongoing epithelial turnover and differentiation.
Basal layer Mitotically active and serves as the regenerative source for the epithelium.

questions.question: Which strain of the HPV virus is responsible for causing Condyloma acuminatum?

explanation.text: Histopathology image suggests Condylomata acuminata, which are benign genital warts caused by low-risk HPV 6 and 11, a double-stranded DNA virus that infects differentiated squamous epithelial cells. It is sexually transmitted and is characterized by multiple, raised, fleshy skin-coloured growths and involves vulvar, vagina, perineal, and perianal regions.

Condyloma acuminata are cauliflower-like, dry, and bulky, typically found in the squamous mucosa of the anal canal. Condyloma lata are smooth, moist, and flat, often located in the genital area, inner thighs, axillae, or oral mucosa. Unlike condyloma acuminata, condyloma lata may appear ulcerated. Microscopic examination reveals papillary, exophytic, treelike stromal cores covered by thickened squamous epithelium.
Koilocytes are evident, featuring enlarged nuclei, hyperchromasia, and a perinuclear cytoplasmic halo. These are not precancerous lesions, and HPV vaccines provide excellent protection.
**HPV 16 and 18 (Option B):** HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk strains responsible for cervical carcinoma, vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia (VIN) and vulvar carcinoma.

questions.question: A 25-year-old sexually active female presents with foul-smelling vaginal discharge and dysuria. Upon examination of the cervix, the following appearance is noted. Wet mount microscopy reveals the findings shown in the image below. Which of the following is most likely responsible for this presentation?

explanation.text: The clinical presentation, examination, and microscopy findings suggest Trichomonas vaginalis infection, a large, flagellated ovoid protozoan transmitted by sexual contact. Patients may present with yellow, frothy vaginal discharge, vulvovaginal discomfort, dysuria (painful urination) dyspareunia (painful intercourse).

The vaginal and cervical mucosa has a fiery-red appearance, with dilation of cervical mucosal vessels resulting in a “strawberry cervix.” Wet mount microscopy of the discharge reveals motile organisms with flagella.

**Candida (Option B):** Clinical features: Curdy white discharge Pap smear: shish kebab effect Herpes simplex virus (Option C) HSV is a sexually transmitted disease characterized by multinucleated squamous cells containing eosinophilic viral inclusions (Cowdry type A inclusions) with a “ground-glass” appearance. The patient presents with painful purulent vesicles/ulcers, often associated with systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and tender inguinal lymph nodes. Clinical features: Painful vesicles. Microscopy: squamous cell nuclei exhibit 3Ms: Multinucleation, molding and margination Human Papillomavirus (Option D) Clinical features: Low risk HPV 6,11 → cause condyloma acuminata. Microscopy; Koilocytes are seen. High risk HPV 16, 18 → cause squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman complains of persistent itching and redness in her vulvar area. On examination, well-defined, erythematous plaques with an eczematous appearance are noted. A biopsy reveals large cells with pale cytoplasm and positive staining for mucopolysaccharides. Immunohistochemical analysis shows positive staining for cytokeratin 7. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Biopsy findings commonly reveal large, round cells, known as Paget cells, within the epidermis. These cells have pale cytoplasm containing mucopolysaccharide that stains with PAS, Alcian blue, or mucicarmine stains. Immunohistochemistry staining often shows positivity for cytokeratin (CK) 7.
Unlike Paget disease of the nipple (Ductal carcinoma of the breast), vulvar Paget's disease is typically not associated with underlying malignancy and is confined to the vulvar epidermis.

questions.question: Which of the following has a strong association with clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina?

options.A: Male partner who has multiple sexual partners
options.D: Sexual activity at a young age

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and biopsy findings suggest Clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina, characterized histologically by cells with clear cytoplasm and hobnail cells and is strongly associated with in-utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES). Vaginal adenosis (precursor lesion for clear cell adenocarcinoma) refers to the presence of glandular columnar epithelium in the proximal vagina.

Diethylstilbestrol is a synthetic non-steroidal estrogen that was historically widely used to prevent potential miscarriages by stimulating the synthesis of estrogen and progesterone in the placenta (especially from the 1940s to the 1970s).

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the pediatric clinic with complaints of vaginal bleeding and a visible mass protruding from her vagina. On examination, a polypoid mass with a "grape-like" appearance is observed. A biopsy is taken, and immunohistochemical staining is positive for desmin. Which of the following will show as a biopsy finding?

options.A: Cells with small protrusions of cytoplasm from one end
options.B: Marked atypia of cells with numerous keratin pearls
options.D: Fibrous stroma covered by mucus-secreting endocervical glands

explanation.text: The clinical presentation and IHC findings suggest Sarcoma botryoides, a rare type of Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, characterised by polypoid,rounded, bulky masses that have the appearance and consistency of grapelike clusters, commonly found in infants and children younger than 5 years of age.

Histologically characterised by cells with small and oval nuclei with small protrusions of cytoplasm resembling a tennis racket (Tennis racket cells/ Tadpole cells) and rarely cytosolic striations (indicative of muscle differentiation) can be seen. The "cambium layer" in sarcoma botryoides refers to a band of undifferentiated or slightly differentiated tumour cells beneath the surface epithelium.

Its presence aids in diagnosing sarcoma botryoides and distinguishing it from other vaginal tumours. Immunohistochemical staining is positive for Desmin/MyoD1. It tends to invade locally and cause death by penetration into the peritoneal cavity obstruction of the urinary tract.

questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of liquid-based cytology (LBC) over the conventional Pap smear?

options.B: More widely available in resource-limited settings

explanation.text: Aspect Conventional Cervical Screening (Pap Smear) Liquid-Based Cytology (LBC) Sample Collection Cells are collected using a spatula or brush and smeared directly onto a glass slide. Cells are collected using a brush and then rinsed into a vial containing a preservative solution. Processing Time Typically longer due to manual preparation and staining. Faster automated processing and staining.

Sensitivity and Specificity Lower sensitivity and specificity compared to LBC. Higher sensitivity and specificity for detecting abnormalities. Cost Generally lower cost. Higher cost due to specialized equipment and supplies. (Option A) Follow-up Testing Additional sample collection may be needed if the initial sample is inadequate.

Usually provides enough samples for additional tests (e.g., HPV testing) without recollection. (Option D) Adequacy of cells 8000-12000 epithelial cells/ 10 hpf (Option C) 5000 epithelial cells/10 hpf Resource limited setting Available in resource-limited settings (Option B) Specialized equipment and infrastructure are needed

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the OPD for regular Pap smear screening. The smear suggests a low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. Which of the following abnormal cell types was most likely seen on the smear?

explanation.text: Koilocytes are abnormal cervical cells seen on pap smears, indicative of HPV infections of the cervix. They are squamous epithelial cells with nuclear enlargement, coarse chromatin, perinuclear cavitation, and irregular nuclear membranes. A rim of condensed cytoplasm often surrounds the perinuclear cavitation, giving the cell a "halo" appearance.

**Doderlein cells (Option A):** Doderlein cells are large, glycogen-rich squamous epithelial cells in the vaginal epithelium, associated with Lactobacillus species. A reduction or absence of Doderlein cells can indicate pathological conditions such as bacterial vaginosis.
**Hobnail cells (Option B):** Hobnail cells are found in clear cell carcinoma of the ovary.

**Arias-Stella reaction cells (Option C):** Arias-Stella reaction cells are a type of glandular epithelial cell found in the endometrium during pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, or pathological conditions like gestational trophoblastic disease.

questions.question: Which of the following risk factors is not typically associated with cervical cancer?

explanation.text: Nulliparity is not a risk factor for cervical cancer. Nulliparity is a risk factor for breast and ovarian cancer.

Risk factors for cervical cancer include: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection, particularly High-risk HPVs, is the most important factor in the development of cervical cancer Multiple sexual partners (Option B) or early sexual activity Smoking (Option A) Weak immune system Long-term use of oral contraceptives (OCP) (Option C) High parity Lack of regular cervical screening (Pap tests) Family history of cervical cancer Socioeconomic factors

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman undergoes a routine gynecological examination. Abnormalities are detected on her pap smear, and colposcopy-guided biopsy reveals dysplastic changes involving two-thirds of the cervical epithelium. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Grade HPE Features CIN 1 Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia with koilocytic atypia showing atypical cells in the lower 1/3rd of the epithelium.

CIN 2 High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL) with progressive atypia and expansion of the immature basal cells in the lower 2/3rd of the epithelial thickness CIN 3 HSIL with diffuse atypia, loss of maturation, and expansion of the immature basal cells to the entire length of the epithelial surface.
**Invasive cervical carcinoma (Option D):** Invasive cervical carcinoma presents with invasion beyond the basement membrane of the cervical epithelium.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix? HPV types 16 and 18 are the most common HPV types identified in invasive cervical cancer. The most common site of metastasis is the lungs. E6 protein interferes with the activity of the tumor suppressor proteins p53. Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common histologic subtype.

explanation.text: Cervical Carcinoma: Squamous cell carcinoma (80%) and adenocarcinoma (15%) are the main cervical cancer subtypes caused by high-risk HPVs (HPV16 and 18). HPV's E6 and E7 proteins disrupt p53 and Rb tumor suppressors, respectively. Lung metastasis is common and indicates poor prognosis. Squamous cell carcinoma:

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman presents with abdominal bloating, discomfort, and increased abdominal girth. Ascites and a palpable pelvic mass are noted on examination. Histopathological examination shows papillary structures with atypical epithelial cells containing psammoma bodies and elevated CA-125 levels. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: The given clinical presentation and histopathological findings point towards diagnosing Serous cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary, characterised by complex papillary structures, psammoma bodies, and atypical epithelial cells with evidence of stromal invasion. Gross morphology shows larger areas of solid or papillary growth, irregularity, and capsule nodularity.
Transvaginal ultrasound shows a large, multicystic mass in the left ovary with papillary projections and solid areas. CA-125 levels are elevated.

questions.question: What is the extent of nonsquamous growth present in Grade 2 endometrial carcinoma?

options.A: 5% or less nonsquamous solid growth pattern

explanation.text: Endometrial carcinoma is of 2 types: 1. Endometrioid carcinoma can be a localised polyp or involve the entire endometrial lining. It demonstrates glandular growth patterns, which fall into 3 grades.

FIGO Grading of endometrial carcinoma Grade 1 5% or less nonsquamous solid growth pattern (well-differentiated) with preserved glandular architecture (Option A) Grade 2 6 - 50% nonsquamous solid growth pattern (moderately differentiated) (Option B) Grade 3 > 50% nonsquamous solid growth pattern (poorly differentiated) (Option C) 2.

Serous carcinomas are seen in atrophic uteri and are often large bulky tumors or deeply invasive into the myometrium. They are distinguished from endometrioid carcinoma by the marked cytologic atypia. They are all Grade 3 tumours and generally have extrauterine spread on the diagnosis.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman presents with irregular vaginal bleeding and passage of grape-like clusters at ten weeks of gestation. Ultrasound reveals a heterogeneous pattern with fetal parts. On histopathology, some villi appear enlarged, and there is a presence of fetal tissue admixed with abnormal placental tissue. Which of the following is true regarding this condition?

explanation.text: This clinical scenario strongly suggests a diagnosis of partial mole, commonly associated with a high risk of invasive mole.

Feature Partial Mole Complete Mole Genetic Origin Normal egg fertilised by more than one sperm Egg with lost chromosomes (empty egg) fertilised by one or two sperms Chromosomal Composition Triploid or occasionally tetraploid Diploid: 90% due to Androgenesis (single sperm duplication); 10% due to Dispermy Fetal Tissue Present Absent Risk of Malignancy High risk of persistent molar disease but not associated with choriocarcinoma High risk of persistent/invasive mole (15%); 2.5% risk of choriocarcinoma Microscopic Features Fraction of villi enlarged, focal trophoblastic hyperplasia All/most villi enlarged, diffuse trophoblastic hyperplasia Immunostaining for p57 Positive (p57 gene is maternally expressed) Negative (p57 gene is paternally imprinted or inactivated)

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman at 11 weeks of gestation presents with vaginal bleeding and passage of grape-like clusters. Ultrasound shows a "snowstorm" appearance without fetal parts. On histopathology, most villi are enlarged with central cistern formation and the absence of fetal tissue. Which of the following is characteristic of this condition?

options.A: Presence of fetal tissue and partially developed placenta
options.B: Diploid karyotype, typically 46, XX or 46, XY, with no fetal tissue
options.C: Triploid karyotype, typically 69, XXX or 69, XXY, with some fetal tissue
options.D: Normal-sized chorionic villi with no trophoblastic proliferation

explanation.text: Clinical scenario points to a diagnosis of a complete mole based on the combination of vaginal bleeding, "snowstorm" appearance on ultrasound, absence of fetal tissue, and histopathology showing diffuse trophoblastic proliferation with hydropic villi.

Complete moles have a diploid karyotype (46, XX or 46, XY), resulting from fertilization of an empty egg by one or two sperm, and lack fetal tissue but exhibit extensive trophoblastic proliferation.Trophoblastic Proliferation: Diffuse and circumferential in complete moles Partial moles typically have a triploid (69, XXX or 69, XXY) or occasionally tetraploid (92, XXXY) karyotype and may contain some fetal tissue along with abnormal placental tissue.
Trophoblastic Proliferation: focal and mild in partial moles.

questions.question: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with progressive abdominal distension, shortness of breath, and pelvic pain. Physical examination reveals ascites and a right-sided pleural effusion. Imaging reveals a solid ovarian mass. A biopsy of the mass shows benign ovarian fibroma. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.text: Meigs syndrome is characterised by the triad of a benign ovarian fibroma, ascites, and pleural effusion (commonly right-sided ).
**Pseudo Meigs syndrome (Option B):** Pseudo-Meigs syndrome is characterised by the triad of ascites, pleural effusion, benign ovarian tumours (other than fibromas), or certain malignant ones.

**Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome (Option C):** Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is a chronic manifestation of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), characterised by inflammation of the liver capsule ( perihepatitis ) without the involvement of liver parenchyma. It leads to adhesion formation leading to violin string appearance in PID accompanied by right upper quadrant pain.

**Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome (Option D):** MRKH syndrome is a congenital condition characterised by the failure of the development of mullerian ducts leading to the absence of the uterus,fallopian tube and upper part of the vagina in otherwise phenotypically normal females with normal ovarian function. It typically presents with primary amenorrhea in teenage girls.

questions.question: Which of the following tumours is typically NOT associated with coffee bean nuclei?

explanation.text: Coffee bean nuclei are characterised by their distinctive longitudinal groove, seen in several tumours, including: Chondroblastoma (Option A) Granulosa cell tumour (Option B) Brenner tumour (Option C) Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) Papillary carcinoma thyroid
